text.p: The price of gold staged a spectacular bounce on Wednesday after it fell to 3-3/4 year lows then speculative funds suddenly came in and bought it.

Gold rose almost $10 to trade above $345 an ounce after it had sunk as low as $336.50 in early European business. The early fall extended a long decline, mainly on fears that other central banks may follow a recent Dutch example and sell bullion from their reserves.
A strong dollar added to the pressure on gold by propping the metal's value in the currencies of nations outside the United States -- when jittery speculators saw a chance to bale out.
But the dollar eased later and investment funds also decided to buy platinum, when the bullion market generally rallied.

New York precious metals futures ended sharply higher, as trade buying and fund short covering rescued gold from a new three year low seen early and end up benefitting the whole complex. COMEX April gold ended up $3.50 an ounce at $345.40, after seeing a five day high intraday at $348.00. In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted at $342.80/30, compared with the London afternoon fix of $337.70.
Industrial metals also staged a modest rally and copper and aluminium ended near the day's highs on the London Metal Exchange.
The rest of the base metals were also boosted higher as short covering and speculative buying lifted sagging prices.

Aluminium ended the afternoon kerb $8 firmer at $1,555 per tonne, having snapped up from support at $1,535 early in the day. That close above $1,550 signalled a chance for consolidation after four days of sharp falls, analysts said.
Copper trundled higher after support at the important $2,200 area held despite protracted tests, traders said.
It ended the afternoon kerb at the important $2,250 level, an increase of $38 from Tuesday, and just below the day's high of $2,555.
CBOT wheat futures closed lower as hopes faded for an increase in wheat exports due to transportation problems in Canada, traders said.
Wheat rallied sharply late Tuesday on fund short covering tied to the traffic tie ups in Canada that led to ideas for a hike in quick shipments of U.S. wheat, mainly spring wheat.
But Asian customers overnight indicated there probably would not be a noticable increase in U.S. wheat exports.
Wheat closed unchanged to 4-3/4 cents per bushel lower, with March down 4-3/4 at $3.57-1/4 a bushel.

NYMEX crude fell Wednesday afternoon after running into technical resistance, reversing gains in refined products which had risen on short covering and spread buying. March crude was off 55 cents a barrel at $21.87.
